title: How do you enforce architectural guardrails as automated tests rather than wiki rules — e.g. ArchUnit rules in CI to forbid synchronous service-to-service calls in a transaction's critical path, forbid dual writes (DB + broker without an outbox), forbid controllers calling repositories directly, and enforce layer/package dependencies — and why does codifying these rules prevent architectural drift across a large team?
shortTitle: How do you enforce architectural guardrails as automated tests rather than wiki rules?

s1_definition.profdef: Architectural guardrails as tests means encoding your architecture's structural rules as executable assertions that run in continuous integration and fail the build when violated, rather than documenting them on a wiki page that developers must remember and reviewers must police by eye. In the JVM world the standard tool is ArchUnit, a Java library that reflects over compiled bytecode and lets you write JUnit tests asserting rules such as controllers must not access repositories directly, services must not call another service synchronously inside a transactional method, no class may write to both a database repository and a message broker without going through an outbox, and package dependencies must flow in one direction only. Because these rules execute on every pull request, they catch violations the moment they are introduced, giving every engineer the same unbendable feedback and preventing the slow erosion of the intended design that otherwise accumulates across a large team.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine the building has rules — tellers never open the vault directly, the loan desk never phones the vault mid-transaction, and no clerk both updates the ledger and mails a letter in one breath without filing an outbox slip. If those rules live only on a laminated poster in the break room, new clerks forget them, busy clerks shortcut them, and over a year the whole bank quietly does the wrong thing. Instead, National Bank installs automatic turnstiles wired to the rules: the moment a clerk tries to open the vault directly, the turnstile locks and a buzzer sounds. ArchUnit is that turnstile for code — the rule is not a suggestion a manager has to catch, it is a gate that physically refuses the violation and stops the day's work until it is fixed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Architectural rules written on a wiki decay silently, but the same rules written as ArchUnit tests in continuous integration fail the build on the first violation, so the architecture is enforced by the machine instead of by human memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Architectural guardrails as tests means encoding your architecture's structural rules as executable assertions that run in continuous integration and fail the build when violated, rather than documenting them on a wiki page that developers must remember and reviewers must police by eye. In the JVM world the standard tool is ArchUnit, a Java library that reflects over compiled bytecode and lets you write JUnit tests asserting rules such as controllers must not access repositories directly, services must not call another service synchronously inside a transactional method, no class may write to both a database repository and a message broker without going through an outbox, and package dependencies must flow in one direction only. Because these rules execute on every pull request, they catch violations the moment they are introduced, giving every engineer the same unbendable feedback and preventing the slow erosion of the intended design that otherwise accumulates across a large team.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine the building has rules — tellers never open the vault directly, the loan desk never phones the vault mid-transaction, and no clerk both updates the ledger and mails a letter in one breath without filing an outbox slip. If those rules live only on a laminated poster in the break room, new clerks forget them, busy clerks shortcut them, and over a year the whole bank quietly does the wrong thing. Instead, National Bank installs automatic turnstiles wired to the rules: the moment a clerk tries to open the vault directly, the turnstile locks and a buzzer sounds. ArchUnit is that turnstile for code — the rule is not a suggestion a manager has to catch, it is a gate that physically refuses the violation and stops the day's work until it is fixed.

**One line to remember:** Architectural rules written on a wiki decay silently, but the same rules written as ArchUnit tests in continuous integration fail the build on the first violation, so the architecture is enforced by the machine instead of by human memory.

sections.s2_technical:
ArchUnit works by loading your compiled classes and giving you a fluent API to express rules over them. The entry point is `ArchRuleDefinition`, and you select classes with `classes()`, filter with `that()`, and assert with `should()`. For example, to forbid controllers from touching repositories directly: `classes().that().resideInAPackage("..controller..").should().onlyDependOnClassesThat().resideOutsideOfPackage("..repository..")`. You attach the scope with `ImportOption` so you only scan your own code and skip test and generated classes. When the rule is violated, ArchUnit throws an `AssertionError` listing every offending class and the exact dependency, so the failure message itself tells the developer what to fix.

To enforce layered architecture end to end, ArchUnit provides a dedicated helper `layeredArchitecture()` where you name each layer and its package, then declare which layers may access which. For a banking service you would write that the controller layer may be accessed by nobody, the service layer may be accessed only by controllers, and the repository layer may be accessed only by services. For example `layeredArchitecture().consideringAllDependencies().layer("Controller").definedBy("..controller..").layer("Service").definedBy("..service..").layer("Repository").definedBy("..repository..").whereLayer("Repository").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service")`. This single rule enforces the entire dependency direction in one place.

Forbidding synchronous service-to-service calls inside a transaction's critical path is a higher-value rule because that pattern holds a database transaction open across a network call, which can block connections and cause cascading timeouts. You express it by finding methods annotated `@Transactional` and asserting they do not call a remote client type. ArchUnit lets you reach method-level detail with `methods().that().areAnnotatedWith(Transactional.class).should(notCallRemoteClients)` where you implement a custom `ArchCondition` that inspects each method's call targets and flags any call into a package like `..client..` or a `RestTemplate`/`WebClient`/`FeignClient` type. For example the condition iterates `method.getCallsFromSelf()` and reports a violation if any target resides in the remote-client package.

Forbidding dual writes without an outbox is the rule that prevents the classic consistency bug where a class saves to the database and publishes to Kafka in the same method, because if the publish fails after the commit, the database and the broker disagree. You write a custom condition that flags any class depending on both a repository type and a broker producer type unless it is the designated outbox relay. For example `noClasses().that().areNotAssignableTo(OutboxRelay.class).should(dependOnBothRepositoryAndBroker)` where the condition checks the class's dependencies for both a `JpaRepository` and a `KafkaTemplate`. This turns an invisible correctness trap into a loud build failure.

Naming conventions and annotation hygiene are also enforceable. You can assert that every class in the service package is annotated `@Service`, that every field injected is final (constructor injection rather than field injection), and that no class uses `java.util.Date` where `java.time` is mandated. For example `fields().that().areDeclaredInClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..service..").should().beFinal()` nudges the whole team toward immutable, test-friendly design.

You wire these into continuous integration simply by making them ordinary JUnit tests in your test source set, so `mvn test` or `gradle test` runs them alongside unit tests, and a violation fails the pipeline exactly like a failing unit test. A senior nuance is to adopt rules incrementally on a large, existing codebase using ArchUnit's `freeze()` capability via `FreezingArchRule`, which records current violations as an accepted baseline and only fails on new violations, so you can stop the bleeding immediately without a giant upfront cleanup, then burn down the baseline over time.

The reason codifying these rules prevents drift is that architecture is a property the whole team must uphold continuously, but humans forget, rotate, and take shortcuts under deadline pressure, and code review catches structural violations inconsistently because reviewers focus on logic. An executable rule is applied identically to every change by every author forever, it documents the intent precisely (the rule is the spec), and it fails fast at the cheapest possible moment, before merge. Over a year across dozens of engineers, that difference is the difference between a clean layered system and an accidental distributed big ball of mud.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's payments platform has grown to forty engineers across six teams, and the architecture is drifting.

Problem 1 — A new controller started calling the repository directly to "save one quick query," bypassing the service layer where validation and auditing live. This is a layering violation; the fix is an ArchUnit layered-architecture rule that fails the build.

Problem 2 — A transfer service method annotated transactional began calling the fraud-check microservice synchronously, holding a database connection open across the network and causing connection-pool exhaustion under load. This is the synchronous-call-in-transaction anti-pattern; the fix is an ArchUnit rule forbidding remote-client calls inside transactional methods.

Problem 3 — A developer saved a transfer to the database and published a Kafka event in the same method, and when Kafka was briefly down the ledger and the event stream disagreed. This is the dual-write trap; the fix is an ArchUnit rule forbidding a class from depending on both a repository and a broker producer unless it is the outbox relay.

We will model a tiny banking codebase with controller, service, repository, client, and broker packages, then write ArchUnit-style rules (implemented here as plain checks so the demo is runnable without the library) that detect each violation, and a demo that scans a "good" design and a "bad" design and reports exactly which rules fail.

The code will have a `CodeModel` representing classes and their dependencies, an `ArchRule` abstraction with concrete rules `LayeringRule`, `NoRemoteCallInTransactionRule`, and `NoDualWriteRule`, a `RuleEngine` that runs all rules and fails on any violation, and a demo that runs the engine against a compliant and a non-compliant module.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two code modules, a compliant "good" module and a non-compliant "bad" module, each a set of classes with their dependencies and annotations.

Step 1 — The rule engine scans the good module. The layering rule checks every controller's dependencies and finds none pointing at a repository, so it passes. The data here is just the class graph; nothing changes, the rule only reads it.

Step 2 — The no-remote-call-in-transaction rule inspects transactional classes in the good module and finds the transfer service depends only on its repository, not on any client, so it passes.

Step 3 — The no-dual-write rule inspects the good module and finds the only class depending on both a repository and a Kafka producer is the outbox relay, which is explicitly exempt, so it passes. The good module reports a clean build.

Step 4 — The engine scans the bad module. The layering rule finds QuickController depends directly on TransferRepository and records a violation with the offending class name.

Step 5 — The no-remote-call rule finds the transactional TransferService depends on FraudClient, a remote client, and records a violation because that holds a transaction open across the network.

Step 6 — The no-dual-write rule finds PaymentService depends on both PaymentRepository and KafkaProducer without being the outbox relay, and records a violation. The engine marks the build failed and prints every violation so the developer fixes them before merge.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Architectural guardrails as tests means I encode the structural rules of my architecture as executable assertions that run in continuous integration and fail the build when violated, instead of documenting them on a wiki that people must remember and reviewers must police by eye. On the JVM the standard tool is ArchUnit, which reflects over my compiled bytecode and lets me write JUnit tests expressing rules in a fluent API, and because these tests run on every pull request, a violation breaks the pipeline exactly like a failing unit test.

The concrete rules I rely on are high value. I forbid controllers from depending on repositories directly so the service layer is never bypassed and validation and auditing always run. I enforce the whole layered dependency direction in one place with ArchUnit's layered-architecture helper. I forbid synchronous remote calls inside transactional methods, because that holds a database connection open across a network call and exhausts the connection pool under load. And I forbid any class from depending on both a repository and a message-broker producer unless it is the designated outbox relay, which stops the dual-write consistency trap where the database commits but the event publish fails and the two stores silently disagree.

I wire these in simply by placing them in the test source set so they run under the normal build command, and a violation fails continuous integration before merge. On a large legacy codebase I adopt them incrementally using ArchUnit's freezing rule, which records the current violations as an accepted baseline and only fails on new ones, so I stop the bleeding immediately and burn the baseline down over time rather than blocking on a giant upfront cleanup.

In my banking platform this mattered because the team had grown to forty engineers and the design was drifting — a controller started calling a repository directly, a transactional transfer method started calling the fraud microservice synchronously, and someone saved to the database and published to Kafka in the same method, which disagreed when Kafka blipped. Each of those would have been caught inconsistently in code review, but as ArchUnit rules they failed the build the moment they were introduced, with the exact offending class named in the failure message.

The reason codifying the rules prevents drift is that architecture is a property the whole team must uphold continuously, and humans forget, rotate, and shortcut under deadline pressure, while an executable rule is applied identically to every change by every author forever, documents the intent precisely because the rule is the specification, and fails at the cheapest possible moment. Over a year across many engineers, that is the difference between a clean layered system and an accidental distributed big ball of mud.
